title: Get To
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. recounts catching himself mid-complaint on his way into school -- "gotta do it, one more day" -- and reflexively correcting it to "get to, not got to," a small linguistic shift that noticeably lifted his mood before the first day of school. He builds three brief arguments for why the reframe is accurate rather than just cheerful self-talk: teaching is never done on pain of death, since every teacher retains real agency to do something else; no one has ever taught the exact combination of students on this year's roster, so the daily work is quietly unprecedented; and the mastery students are working toward, whatever the subject, is an unambiguous good that enriches their lives. He ties the piece back to a recurring theme -- that clear thinking means partnering with reality rather than resisting it -- and argues that "get to" is simply a more accurate description of a teacher's actual circumstances than "got to," not merely a more pleasant one.
points: The reframe from "got to" to "get to" is argued to be more accurate, not just more positive, because teaching is never actually compulsory -- every teacher retains real agency to do something else, which makes staying a genuine choice.

The claim that "no one has ever taught the group of students you get to teach this year" reframes an ordinary school year as a quietly unrepeatable, unprecedented event, even though it won't register as historic to anyone outside the room.

Stuart connects the reframe to his recurring principle that reduced teacher stress comes from "partnering with reality" rather than resisting it, positioning "get to" as clearer thinking rather than forced positivity.

The piece models a low-cost, repeatable practice -- catching and correcting one's own language in the moment -- as a legitimate lever for daily teacher morale, not requiring any structural or schedule change.
quotes: It was so cheesy (and so ridiculous that I was talking to myself as I walked into school) that I softly chuckled. But for whatever reason — the internal self-deprecation, the absurdity of muttering motivational bumper stickers to yourself while you walk into your workplace, a genuine mental shift from got to to get to — the moment helped.

Not one of us teaches on pain of death. Like I wrote last spring, we could do something else besides teaching. All of us could. Our degree of agency varies by the person, but the reality of a teacher's agency is universal.

No one has ever taught the group(s) of students you get to teach this year. Even if you taught the same exact group of people last year — they're different this year. There's never been a combination of people exactly like the one you have on your roster.

The mastery you're after helping students achieve this year — in computers, in calculus, in decoding a text, in describing an experiment, in running the mile, in reading primary sources — is the kind of thing that can enrich the lives of every one of your students.
I said some time ago that the closer we get to partnering with reality in our classrooms, the less stressed out we'll be. That's the goal of clear thinking: partnership with reality.
